title: What Is Ontology (Preview)? - Microsoft Fabric | Microsoft Learn
summary: Microsoft Learn's architectural deep dive on the ontology (preview) item that anchors Fabric IQ: how enterprise vocabulary is modeled as entity types, entity instances, properties, and relationships, how that model is bound to live data in OneLake/lakehouses/eventhouses/semantic models to form a queryable instance graph, and how natural-language and structured queries traverse that graph.
audience: Solution architects and data modelers designing a shared semantic/ontology layer over an existing lakehouse or warehouse estate, and anyone evaluating how Fabric IQ's ontology differs from a Power BI semantic model or a plain graph database.
why_it_matters: The existing fabric-iq-overview source only established L1 concepts (that an ontology item exists and pairs with semantic models). This source supplies the L3 architectural detail on how the ontology's logical model (entity types/properties/relationships) is actually materialized against OneLake data as a queryable instance graph, which is the missing link needed before architecture or learning content can explain how to design one.
takeaways: An ontology is structured as three coupled layers: a logical vocabulary (entity types, properties, relationships), a data-binding layer that attaches that vocabulary to real OneLake/eventhouse/semantic-model data, and a queryable instance graph built from those bindings.
Entity types intentionally sit above any single table so that column-level definitions can vary by source while the business concept stays singular and reusable.

The ontology graph is a distinct, dependent Fabric item (built on Graph in Microsoft Fabric) rather than a virtual view — it stores materialized nodes/edges with lineage and requires the tenant's Graph capability to be enabled.

Query execution is federated and engine-routed: the ontology layer pushes a single business-level query down to whichever backend actually holds the data (GQL against Graph, KQL against Eventhouse), rather than requiring the caller to know the storage engine.

NL2Ontology translates natural-language questions into structured queries constrained by the published ontology's definitions, so units, join paths, and validity windows stay aligned with governed meaning rather than being inferred ad hoc by an LLM.

claims.text: An ontology in Fabric IQ is composed of entity types (the things), properties (their facts), and relationships (how they connect), together with constraints and rules that keep those representations consistent across teams.

An entity type is a reusable logical model of a real-world concept that standardizes name, description, identifiers, properties, and constraints, deliberately elevated above any single table so that inconsistent per-source column definitions don't fragment the concept's meaning.

An entity instance is a concrete, timestamped occurrence of an entity type populated from a data binding; it retains which source created it and when it was true, letting raw rows become standardized, provenance-tracked business objects.

Relationships in the ontology are typed, directional links between entity types or instances that can carry their own attributes (e.g., distance, confidence, effective-at) and cardinality rules, making traversal and dependency analysis possible without hand-written join logic.

Data binding is the layer that connects an ontology's entity types, properties, and relationships to concrete OneLake data — lakehouse tables, eventhouse streams, or Power BI semantic models — by mapping columns to properties and keys to relationship links, while carrying schema-evolution rules, data-quality checks, and provenance at the concept level.

The ontology graph is a queryable instance graph — nodes as entity instances, edges as asserted or derived links with metadata — built on top of the separate Graph in Microsoft Fabric item, which must be enabled as a tenant setting before an ontology's graph features work.

Ontology queries start from an entity type and let a caller filter by property, traverse relationships, and aggregate over time using business terminology; the ontology layer then routes execution to whichever backend holds the data, such as GQL for Graph in Microsoft Fabric or KQL for Eventhouse.

NL2Ontology converts natural-language business questions into structured ontology queries and constrains the generated filters, joins, units, and validity windows to the definitions published in the ontology, rather than letting a model infer them freely from raw schema.

Upstream data source changes (new, updated, or deleted rows) are not automatically reflected in an ontology's bound data or graph — they require an explicit manual or scheduled refresh of the graph model before they become visible.
